title: Act II, Scene III

teacherSummary.text: A drunken Porter imagines himself porter of hell gate, joking about a farmer, an 'equivocator' and a tailor, before opening to Macduff and Lennox. Lennox describes an unruly night of storms and screams. Macduff discovers Duncan's body ('Confusion now hath made his masterpiece!'). Macbeth reveals he has killed the chamberlains, claiming fury and love; Lady Macbeth faints. Banquo vows to fight 'treasonous malice.' Malcolm and Donalbain secretly flee to England and Ireland, fearing 'daggers in men's smiles.'

writingPrompts.label: Middle School
writingPrompts.text: Excerpt-based (Middle School support track; this play is above the grades 6–8 complexity band, so work from the passage your teacher selects). In “Act II, Scene III,” how does Shakespeare show the discovery of the murder? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the passage, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the irony you noticed as one piece of evidence.

writingPrompts.label: HS Freshman
writingPrompts.text: In Act II, Scene III, how does Shakespeare develop the idea of the discovery of the murder? State a clear claim, support it with two or three quotations, and explain how the irony in the scene helps build that idea.

writingPrompts.label: HS Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how Act II, Scene III develops the idea of the discovery of the murder. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of irony and tone / mood shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.

writingPrompts.label: HS Junior
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how the structure of Act II, Scene III (where it begins, turns and ends) and its irony shape the reader's understanding of the discovery of the murder. Identify one place where the text leaves matters uncertain and explain how that uncertainty adds to its meaning. Distinguish what is directly stated from what is really meant.

writingPrompts.label: HS Senior
writingPrompts.text: Two readers disagree about what Act II, Scene III suggests about the discovery of the murder. Lay out two plausible interpretations, weigh the evidence for each (including the scene's irony and tone / mood), and argue for the stronger one in a sustained, well-organized essay. Distinguish what is directly stated from what is really meant.

writingPrompts.label: AP
writingPrompts.text: Write a literary argument in which you analyze how William Shakespeare uses irony in Act II, Scene III to complicate the reader's understanding of the discovery of the murder. Develop a defensible thesis, select evidence purposefully, and explain how specific choices of diction and syntax create meaning.

writingPrompts.label: College Freshman
writingPrompts.text: Situate Act II, Scene III within its historical and literary context and argue how the scene's treatment of the discovery of the murder responds to that context. Engage with at least one secondary perspective (a critic, historian or the author's own statements), integrate quotations smoothly, and cite in MLA style.

writingPrompts.label: College Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Read Act II, Scene III alongside the conventions of its genre and period. Argue how the scene's handling of the discovery of the murder follows or bends those conventions, using the irony as evidence, and test your reading against one published critic. Document two secondary sources in MLA.

writingPrompts.label: College Junior
writingPrompts.text: Apply a named critical approach (for example formalist, historicist, feminist, psychoanalytic or ecocritical) to Act II, Scene III and its treatment of the discovery of the murder. State your method, show what it reveals in the scene's irony and tone / mood, and identify where the text resists it.

writingPrompts.label: College Senior
writingPrompts.text: Develop a research argument that reads Act II, Scene III as evidence for a larger claim about the discovery of the murder in Macbeth. Connect close reading of the scene to the whole play, engage at least four scholarly sources, and state precisely where your reading departs from theirs (Chicago style).

writingPrompts.label: Graduate / PhD
writingPrompts.text: Develop an original argument that reads Act II, Scene III as a hinge in the play's larger treatment of the discovery of the murder. Position your reading within a named critical conversation (for example formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist or postcolonial approaches), account for the textual history where relevant, and articulate the stakes of your intervention for scholarship on Macbeth.

segments.activity: Respond in writing to the bell-ringer, then pair-share.
segments.script: Settle in and write for five minutes: Why might a writer place a joke right after a terrible event? No wrong answers yet; we will test these ideas against the text. Two volunteers share, and I note key words on the board.

segments.activity: Introduce 5 key words: pronounce, define from context, then the word's history.
segments.script: Today's words are primrose, napkins, bonfire, masterpiece, sacrilegious. For each one we read the sentence, guess from context and then check the definition. Here is the first: “I’ll devil-porter it no further: I had thought to have let in some of all professions that go the primrose way to the everlasting bonfire.” In this sentence it means: pleasant and easy (the primrose way is the easy path of pleasure). Word histories: For the other words, look up the word history (Etymonline or the OED) and record the language of origin and the root meaning in your etymology log.

segments.activity: Present the historical and literary background.
segments.script: Here is what the first readers of Macbeth would have known. The Porter's 'equivocator' is widely read as an allusion to the Jesuit Henry Garnet, executed in 1606 after the Gunpowder Plot, who defended misleading answers under oath. Why does this scene matter? Comic relief deepens the horror: the castle has become hell's gate. Macbeth's killing of the grooms removes witnesses and makes his own guilt more visible; the princes' flight lets suspicion fall on them. Write down one question you want answered.

segments.activity: Teacher models a think-aloud on the anchor passage for irony.
segments.script: Watch me read this the way a careful reader does. The passage opens: “Marry, sir, nose-painting, sleep, and urine.” I stop and ask: what is the author doing here, and how does it connect to the discovery of the murder? I circle “provoke”, one of today's words, and ask why the author chose it over a plainer word. When I find irony, I underline it and write its effect in the margin, then I check my idea against the next sentence.

segments.activity: Read the anchor passage aloud together; annotate for irony.
segments.script: Now we do it together. I read the first sentence and you track along. Mark every example of irony. Turn to a partner: what does the author want us to notice? I will collect three ideas and we choose the strongest using evidence.
segments.passage: Marry, sir, nose-painting, sleep, and urine. Lechery, sir, it provokes, and unprovokes; it provokes the desire, but it takes away the performance: therefore, much drink may be said to be an equivocator with lechery: it makes him, and it mars him; it sets him on, and it takes him off; it persuades him, and disheartens him; makes him stand to, and not stand to; in conclusion, equivocates him in a sleep, and, giving him the lie, leaves him.

segments.activity: Students annotate a new passage independently in the reader, then begin the writing prompt at their assigned rigor level.
segments.script: Your turn. Annotate the next page in the app for Irony, Tone / mood, Plot: at least three marks with a margin note each. Then open your writing prompt; the app shows the level your teacher assigned (for a 9–10 class, the HS Sophomore prompt reads: Analyze how Act II, Scene III develops the idea of the discovery of the murder. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of irony and tone / mood shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.) I will circulate and conference.

segments.activity: Structured discussion from the 30 tiered questions (focus set for the class level): wait time, think-pair-share on DOK 3/4, follow-up probes.
segments.script: Let's talk. We move from what happens to why it matters to whether it's right. After each question I wait before calling on anyone: think first. Our anchor question: How does this scene connect to ambition and its costs? Every claim needs a page reference. Respond to the person before you by agreeing, extending or challenging with evidence, and end by writing one question of your own.

segments.activity: Scene quiz in the app, then a one-sentence exit ticket.
segments.script: Take the scene quiz in the app. Then, in one sentence, tell me what this scene suggests about the discovery of the murder, backed by one short quotation.

segments.activity: Summarize the lesson and preview the next reading.
segments.script: Today we saw how irony shapes the discovery of the murder. Tonight, read the next scene and add two words to your etymology log.

routine: Bell-ringer: post one literal and one evaluative question; students jot before talking (wait time).
Discussion (10 min): run the focus questions for the class level in order, literal to evaluative; think-pair-share every DOK 3/4 item.
After each answer, use a follow-up probe before moving on; ask a second student to agree, extend or challenge.
Exit: each student writes one question of their own (student-generated) for tomorrow’s opener.

middleSchool.note: Excerpt-based: read the passage aloud first; use the scaffolds; accept partial answers and build with probes.

hsFreshman.note: Use the scaffolds for literal and inferential items; require one quotation for every inferential answer.

hsSophomore.note: Require a quotation and an explanation; push evaluative answers to address a counterclaim.

hsJunior.note: Emphasize structure and ambiguity; students should name where the text leaves matters open.

hsSenior.note: Weigh competing interpretations; students should defend the stronger reading.

ap.note: Treat each evaluative item as a thesis rehearsal: defensible claim, purposeful evidence, commentary on choices.

collegeFreshman.note: Add the extension: connect answers to historical context and one secondary perspective.

collegeSophomore.note: Use the extensions: genre and period conventions, and a published critic.

collegeJunior.note: Use the extensions: name a critical method and test it against the passage.

collegeSenior.note: Use the extensions: connect the scene to the whole work and the scholarship.

graduate.note: Use the extensions: position answers in a critical conversation and the textual history.
